title: EAS Payments (engine-first slice)
description: A learning/prototype vertical slice of the EAS Payments Engine on Snapback. A store notification is a thin trigger: the action re-fetches authoritative transaction state from a fake local store over ctx.fetch with a granted ctx.secrets credential, then commits through one mutation. entitlementGrants is derived from all of a user's transactions and backs the live query the app gates on. The symmetric outbound half is a change feed carrying only { userId, seq } that a developer polls with a keyset cursor before re-reading authoritative entitlements themselves.

backend.stalenessPolicy: committed review manifest; regenerate with codegen under SNAPBACK_OUTBOUND_ACTIONS=1 (the opt-in is a codegen input and changes inputsHash); freshness tracked by artifacts.json inputsHash

headless.toolchain: node>=22 (built-in fetch); cargo to build/run the local server; the suite starts its own fake store and fake developer endpoint

notClaiming: real store validation — validateReceipt and applyStoreState perform real outbound fetches, but against a fake local store fixture, not Apple/Google/Stripe, and with no signature or JWS verification
production auth — the slice runs in dev auth mode; sessions mode is out of scope
system-authority fencing for the reconcile path — reconcileTransaction takes userId as an argument because a store notification carries no session, and dev auth cannot restrict it to system authority
webhook body signing — the ping authenticates the sender with a shared-secret bearer but does not bind the payload; the handler surface exposes no digest primitive to build an HMAC with
SSRF fencing — webhook endpoint registration checks only the http/https scheme, not loopback or link-local targets

concurrency-safe change-feed sequencing — seq is minted read-max-plus-one inside the mutation; ctx.sequence.allocate exists but permits one allocation per mutation, and the expiry sweep appends a row per user in one commit
metering or billing — transactions carry an environment tag so sandbox rows can be excluded later, and nothing consumes it yet

time-aware grant derivation: deriveGrant reads lifecycle states and horizons but never compares them to the clock, so the expiry sweep is the single horizon enforcer. If the store still reports 'grace' with a graceUntil that already passed, a redundant applyStoreState re-grants the access the sweep just retired, until the next sweep undoes it. Bounded by one cron interval (60s declared) and asserted in both directions by the acceptance rather than hidden

real store lifecycle mapping: the seven states are the engine's normalized vocabulary, not a verified translation of Apple's, Google's, and Stripe's own status models, which differ from each other and carry states this slice does not model (billing retry sub-phases, upgrade/downgrade proration, family sharing)
